# This Cover Image Was Generated by an Agent (I Built the One That Made It)

*Every cover image on my recent articles — including this one — was generated by a small open-source agent I built. One reasoning pass, one image call, everything else deterministic.*

---

## The phone call that triggered this article

Yesterday my article **"Job Hunting Is a Data Problem (I Treated It Like One)"** crossed **1,200+ impressions in a single day** — by far the strongest response I've had on LinkedIn.

Then a friend called. He liked the article, but couldn't resist a joke: *"Nice cover image — did you borrow my company's website color theme?"*

It was pure coincidence. But it was also the perfect excuse to write this post, because that cover — and every cover on my recent articles — wasn't designed in Canva or prompted in a chat window. It was generated by an agent I open-sourced in the same repo as the job-scout pipeline: **`linkedin-cover-generator`**, built on **Vercel's Eve agentic framework**.

And to answer my friend properly: the agent ships with **seven baked-in color palettes** (plus `auto` mode that deliberately avoids repeating the previous run's palette). His company's theme just happened to be one roll of the dice.

## From a ChatGPT project to a real agent

For a long time, my workflow was a ChatGPT web project: paste the article, iterate on prompts, download, check dimensions, repeat. It worked, but it was manual, unrepeatable, and every image was a one-off negotiation.

When I found **Eve** — Vercel's agent framework that quietly powers hundreds of their internal infrastructure agents — I rebuilt the whole thing as code: an orchestrator, deterministic tools, a Docker sandbox, and full observability on every run. There are surprisingly few fully functional, working Eve agents in the public domain right now (the framework is that new), which is exactly why I'm sharing this one.

## The architecture: one judgment call, everything else is a tool

The same principle from my job-scout pipeline applies here: **models step in only when judgment is needed. Typed, deterministic tools do everything else.**

Each run follows a fixed path:

1. **Load the input** — local markdown file, remote URL, or pasted text (Readability + gray-matter for clean extraction)
2. **One orchestrator reasoning pass** — the only creative model call. It reads the article and emits a `cover-spec.json`: title, subtitle, palette, layout, visual concept, all validated against a Zod schema
3. **Build the image prompt** — deterministic. No model call. The prompt is constructed from the spec by code
4. **One image generation call** — the cover itself
5. **Validate dimensions** — deterministic pixel check with sharp. LinkedIn presets baked in (article 1280×720, profile banner 1584×400, post, carousel, square)
6. **Assemble the report** — timing, tokens, and cost computed by a tool, not an LLM. Every run folder gets `report.md` + `summary.json`

**No unbounded review loop. No retry-until-it-looks-right.** `ENABLE_REVIEW=false` and `MAX_IMAGE_RETRIES=0` by default. If you want a reviewer pass or a retry on hard failure, you opt in explicitly — bounded to one.

## Two cheap models, full control

The whole thing runs on two inexpensive models, configured independently and fully env-driven (no hard-coded defaults):

```dotenv
MODEL_ORCHESTRATOR=claude-sonnet-5   # one bounded cover-spec pass
IMAGE_MODEL=gpt-image-2              # the image itself
```

The report tool tells me exactly what each cover costs. That's the point of pushing work out of models and into deterministic tools: **the bill and the behavior both become predictable.**

## Options without prompt archaeology

Everything is a typed option in the request, not a prompt trick:

- `palette=charcoal-gold-teal` (or `indigo-lime`, `navy-cyan-violet`, `cream-emerald`… or `auto`)
- `size=linkedin-article` or any custom `WxH` (auto-snapped to multiples of 16 for the image API)
- `layout=centered-minimal`, `density=balanced`
- `approval=true` — the agent writes the spec and a proposal, then **stops** for your review before spending a single image token
- `include_brands=false` by default — brand safety is a skill file, not an afterthought

## Why Eve — and why this is bigger than cover images

These agents aren't side projects for their own sake. They are my **hands-on evaluation lab** for a much bigger move: preparing my entire team to shift our automations toward **agentic development under the AI-DLC methodology** (Intent → Mob elaboration → Units of work → Bolt → Deployment unit → Production).

My conviction: **don't retrofit GenAI into conventional development.** Bolting a chat call onto an existing SDLC gives you conventional software with an expensive dependency. The right move is to *unlearn* and approach the lifecycle fresh with AI-DLC — where intent drives the spec, models handle judgment, and deterministic tools carry the execution.

To pick the framework for that journey, I built real, working agents on **Pi, Flue, LangChain, and Eve** — not slide-deck comparisons, actual running code. Eve won on four criteria that matter in an enterprise setting:

- **Workflow as a first-class concept** — not just a loop of tool calls
- **Wait / pause for human-in-the-loop** — approval gates are native (you saw it above: `approval=true` stops the run before a single image token is spent)
- **Full observability** — every run traced, tokens and cost accounted, artifacts synced
- **Deploys on-prem *and* cloud/SaaS** — the same agent runs in a local Docker sandbox or on Vercel infrastructure

The cover generator is the proof-of-learning. The destination is a team that builds this way by default.

## Try it

Full code, design docs (`DESIGN.md`, ADRs), and a shared agent-runtime kit (model resolution, usage hooks, cost matrix, sandbox base) are in the monorepo:

**github.com/senthilsweb/ai-agents** → `agents/linkedin-cover-generator/`

```bash
nvm use 24
npm install
npx eve dev --port 3535
# then: Create a LinkedIn cover from input=inputs/article.md, palette=auto
```

If you're exploring Eve, or trying to figure out where the line between "model decides" and "tool executes" should sit in your own agents — this is a small, complete, working example.

*Spec first. Typed tools do the work. Models step in only when judgment is needed.*
